posts.text: 🌍 BE/B.Tech CSE Done. Should You Consider Studying Abroad? For a CSE graduate, studying abroad can be more than earning another degree. It can be an opportunity to gain global tech exposure, deeper specialization, research experience and a different way of solving engineering problems. Universities across the USA, UK, Germany, Canada, Australia, Singapore and other technology hubs offer postgraduate programs in areas such as AI/ML, Cloud Computing, Cybersecurity, Robotics, Data Science and Software Engineering. 💻 What can you gain? 🔹 Specialization — Go deeper into AI, ML, Cloud, Cybersecurity, Robotics, etc. 🔹 Research Exposure — Work on advanced technologies and real research problems 🔹 Industry Projects — Apply classroom knowledge to practical challenges 🔹 Global Collaboration — Work with students and professionals from different countries 🔹 Internships & Networking — Access university career networks and industry connections 🔹 Communication Skills — Learn to work in multicultural engineering teams 🔹 Different Tech Ecosystems — Experience how companies build products at global scale 🚀 What could the path look like? BE/B.Tech CSE → MS/MTech/MSc specialization → Projects + Research → Internship → Global Tech Experience Possible specializations: 🤖 AI & Machine Learning ☁️ Cloud & Distributed Systems 🔐 Cybersecurity 📊 Data Science 💻 Software Engineering 🦾 Robotics & Autonomous Systems ⚡ Semiconductor & Systems 🌐 Product Engineering But there is an important reality: Going abroad does not automatically create a great tech career. The current international CS job market is competitive, particularly for entry-level roles, and visa/work authorization can significantly affect opportunities. Recent reporting also shows that AI is changing traditional software-development hiring. So the goal shouldn't simply be: “I want to study abroad.” It should be: “I want to become a stronger engineer with global exposure.” Build strong DSA + programming + projects + internships + communication skills before you leave. Then use the international degree to add specialization, research, industry exposure and global perspective. 🌍 A foreign university can open doors. Your skills are what help you walk through them. #CSE #ComputerScience #StudyAbroad #TechCareers #MSinCS #IT #AI #MachineLearning #CloudComputing #SoftwareEngineering #GlobalTech #EngineeringStudents #CareerGrowth

posts.text: Pakistan’s IT exports hit a record $4.6B in FY2025–26. Great news. But there’s another side developers must watch: AI is reshaping what global clients pay for. Research from the Pakistan Business Council shows the median freelance transaction fell 41% between FY2021 and FY2025, even as total freelance exports more than doubled. More work is leaving Pakistan, but typical deals are smaller. Now add AI. Global firms increasingly use AI coding agents to automate parts of software development. Some bring work in-house they once outsourced. Outsourcing isn’t disappearing—its economics are changing. For years, Pakistan’s edge was simple: good talent at lower cost. But what happens when AI reduces the human hours needed for the same output? A client who once needed 3 developers × 160 hours may now need fewer people and fewer hours. The developer isn’t less capable—billable human work has changed. Routine tasks face the most pricing pressure: Basic websites Simple CRUD apps Repetitive integrations Basic testing & bug fixes Data entry Generic content This work isn’t vanishing overnight, but margins are shrinking. There’s another risk: the junior pipeline. If firms produce more with fewer entry-level developers, how will new talent gain experience to become senior? That said, AI won’t take all jobs. New demand is emerging in: AI integration Cloud infrastructure Data engineering Cybersecurity System architecture AI-enabled products Engineers who can implement and maintain these systems in production are in demand. The market isn’t just shrinking—it’s shifting. Pakistani developers shouldn’t respond by becoming cheaper. The opportunity is to move up the value chain. I use AI daily—it makes me faster—but it doesn’t understand the client’s business, make architectural trade-offs, explain production incidents, or take the 3am call. That part of engineering is becoming more important, not less. Pakistan’s IT opportunity is growing, but selling cheaper developer hours is losing power. The next advantage will be: AI + engineering judgment + domain knowledge + ownership. What are you seeing? Are global clients hiring fewer developers, or expecting the same developers to deliver more with AI? #Pakistan #SoftwareEngineering #AI #TechCareers #FutureOfWork

posts.text: Every few years marketing decides it wants to be engineering when it grows up. In 2010 we got the growth hacker. In 2023 Clay gave us the GTM engineer. And this April, Profound's co-founder put "marketing engineer" on a slide at his own company's conference, and at least one guy in the audience updated his LinkedIn title before the keynote was over. Respect, honestly. Six months later the marketing engineer has a manifesto, a university course, a job board, a hackathon and a podcast. Profound made all five. Actual hires? Around 173 in the past year, according to Live Data Technologies. You could seat the entire profession at a mid-sized wedding. I'm not saying the work is fake. Marketing teams really are building agents to do competitor research and buy media, and plenty of companies are rebuilding their sites so ChatGPT stops describing them wrong. Somebody has to build and run that stuff. But I'd watch who's doing the defining. GTM engineer became a real job once people with nothing to sell started writing about it. Salary surveys, newsletters, bootcamps someone doesn't own. Growth hacker went the other way. The methods got so normal that the title stopped meaning anything, and nobody really missed it. Marketing engineer hasn't hit either point yet. Right now it belongs to one software company, and the employers hiring for it can't even agree on whether they want a developer with three years of experience or the CRM person who was already automating everything in Zapier. Our guess is this ends the way growth hacking did. In a few years every good marketer builds things, and "marketing engineer" sounds about as dated as "social media guru". So the question is no longer: “Will software engineering teams become leaner?” I think they will. The more interesting question is: What kind of engineer will still be worth hiring? My rough expectation: 2026–2027: Hiring continues, but the bar rises sharply. Junior and CRUD-heavy roles get hit hardest. Companies increasingly ask: “Why do we need 8 engineers here instead of 3 strong engineers + agents?” 2027–2029: Significant compression. Teams that once needed 10–15 engineers may operate (or already operaing) with 4–8 strong engineers supported by agents. 2029–2032: If agent reliability keeps improving, the role of a “software engineer whose primary output is code” becomes much smaller. But I don’t think the future engineer is simply someone monitoring AI agents. The valuable engineer starts looking more like: Problem owner → Architect → Agent orchestrator → Reviewer → Production owner Instead of spending hours implementing an API, you might tell agents: “We need a pricing service with these business constraints, latency requirements, security boundaries, and rollback guarantees.” Agents can explore designs, write code, tests, migrations, inspect telemetry, and propose deployments. Your job becomes deciding: What should exist? Which constraints actually matter? Which trade-offs are acceptable? Is the agent solving the right problem, or just producing technically correct code? This is why I think experienced engineers may actually become more valuable. AI has absorbed a huge amount of knowledge that once differentiated senior engineers. But knowledge was never the entire value of a senior engineer. The real value was judgment, context, trade-offs, ownership, understanding messy business requirements, and being accountable when things go wrong. I also think the middle may get squeezed more than the top. A team of 30 engineers could eventually become 7–10 strong engineers + many agents. Not everywhere. But increasingly plausible. Which is why I would optimize around becoming the engineer who can be given: “We want to launch this business capability.” …and can turn that into architecture, systems, infrastructure, deployment, monitoring, and iteration. DSA and system design will still matter. But long term, the ability to own outcomes and build complete systems using AI as leverage may compound much more strongly. Looking at how quickly coding agents have improved, I would treat the next 2–4 years as the critical transition period for software engineers. Not because engineers disappear by 2030. But because by then the industry may have largely decided: what kind of engineer is still worth hiring. #SharingThoughts #AIAgents #SoftwareEngineering

posts.text: The worst time to hire engineers is the week your round closes, which is exactly when the pressure to start is highest. By then the board has seen the hiring plan and the recruiters are lined up. What the hiring plan rarely shows is that the engineers you already have are about to onboard everyone you hire, right when they're also being asked to deliver what the round promised. Good engineers can build whatever roadmap you hand them. What they can't do is onboard themselves. Every new hire needs time from your best engineers, priorities that hold still long enough to learn the work, and a team that already ships on a rhythm they can join. The week after a raise is when all three are scarcest. None of this is an argument against hiring. You raised the money to hire, and I've hired plenty myself, from the days of leading four engineers at RainKing through my time as CTO at DiscoverOrg/ZoomInfo. If I were in your seat, I'd open the searches on day one, since the right engineers take a while to find, and use those weeks to get the team ready before the first ones start. That first month is for deciding what the bigger team will work on. Talk to customers about what's next, pick the one or two things that matter most this year, and write down what won't get built, so the priorities hold still when people start arriving. In the second month, I'd make sure I was seeing working software every week, because a team that ships weekly is more likely to absorb new people than one that doesn't. I'd also have the team build the support new engineers will need, so they lean on it instead of your best people. That means documentation for the parts of the system that live only in someone's head, and a review process tight enough to catch a new engineer's mistakes before a customer does. By the third month, I'd be hiring at the pace the team can absorb, and I'd know what each product costs to build and run. I could show the board what we're building, why customers want it and when it will ship, next to the hiring numbers. A round buys runway, and the first 90 days decide how far it takes you. If you've been through a raise as a founder, an engineer or an investor, what would you tell a CEO whose round closed last week? #SaaS #ProductStrategy #VentureCapital

posts.headline: CTO at CircleCI
posts.text: In a recent podcast with Josh Anderson of Revelo, we got onto the topic of why I'm having such great results with hiring junior developers right now. Historically, we brought junior engineers in and trained them in the shape of senior engineers. The problem is, though, we’re not totally sure what that shape is anymore. The job is changing quickly. We’re spending less time writing syntax and more time thinking about systems, building tools that build software, and figuring out where humans need to be involved (if at all). In some ways, all that change is a great leveler. A new grad isn’t transitioning from an old way of working to a new one, they’re just learning how the job works now. That fresh perspective is extremely useful when so many of our old assumptions are up for debate. They ask why we do something a certain way, and sometimes the answer is, “I have no idea. It’s just how we’ve always done it.” That’s been a huge part of what makes our new grad program work. We’re learning alongside them, and getting a ton of energy, curiosity, and fresh ways of looking at things in return. There's amazing talent out there in the new grad pool. I cant recommend it enough.

posts.text: Computer science is just the history of pushing human beings up the abstraction ladder. In the 1950s, we manually punched 1s and 0s into cards. Then assembly gave us readable instructions for hardware. Then compiled languages decoupled us from machine architectures entirely. Now, natural language models are decoupling us from routine syntax. Every generation of engineers feared that abstraction would destroy their value. Every time, it did the exact opposite: it freed them to solve bigger problems. When high level languages became standard, companies stopped asking candidates to manage memory registers by hand. We realized that human judgment belonged at the system design layer, not the hardware execution layer. So why are we still treating algorithmic puzzles like DSA as the gold standard for software engineering competence? AI produces syntax effortlessly. What it cannot do is understand company context, business risk, or domain nuance. The next generation of senior engineers will not be implementers. They will be Domain Translators: * Business acumen first: Understanding why a feature needs to exist before asking how to write it. * Precision in specification: Defining edge cases, constraints, and architecture with ruthless clarity. * Critical evaluation: Auditing generated logic against real world production realities. The barrier to entry for writing code is collapsing to zero. The premium on knowing what to build and why has never been higher. #TechLeadership #SoftwareEngineering #GenerativeAI #Hiring #FutureOfWork
